findings.proposedIrEvidence: rules[0].conditions contains only condition[0]: conditionType UNSUPPORTED, description "The exception for the Disposition of obsolete or worn out property applies only if the disposition occurs in the ordinary course of business"; capacityExpression is UNLIMITED_CAPACITY with gatedBy null; sufficiency is COMPLETE.
findings.sourceEvidence: (a) the Disposition of obsolete or worn out property in the ordinary course of business;
findings.verifierReasoning: The source carve-out contains two independent qualifiers: the property must be 'obsolete or worn out property' AND the disposition must be 'in the ordinary course of business.' The proposed IR models only the ordinary-course qualifier as a condition; the 'obsolete or worn out' limitation appears only inside the prose description of the exception, not as a modeled restriction. A consumer applying the IR could conclude that a disposition of any property in the ordinary course of business is permitted by 7.5(a), which is not what the source says. For example, a sale of new, non-obsolete equipment in the ordinary course would satisfy the represented condition but is outside the source exception. This is a material scope difference, and the COMPLETE sufficiency claim makes the omission more serious.

findings.proposedIrEvidence: The rule has "dependsOn": [] and the IR has "definitions": [], so neither the defined term "Disposition" nor "Property" is carried into the representation.
findings.sourceCitation: Definition of "Disposition" (retrieved context); see also definition of "Property" (any right or interest in or to property of any kind whatsoever, whether real, personal or mixed and whether tangible or intangible, including Capital Stock).
findings.sourceEvidence: "Disposition": with respect to any Property, any sale, lease, sale and leaseback, assignment, conveyance, transfer or other disposition thereof (whether effected pursuant to a Division or otherwise). The terms "Dispose" and "Disposed of" shall have correlative meanings.
findings.verifierReasoning: Section 7.5(a) turns on the defined term 'Disposition' and on the defined scope of 'Property.' The IR's machine-readable portion does not preserve these definitional dependencies, so a user relying on the IR alone cannot know that the exception covers leases, sale-leasebacks, assignments, conveyances, transfers, and divisions, not merely sales, or that Property includes rights in Capital Stock. This is a missing dependency rather than an affirmative misstatement. I cannot fully resolve whether the intended IR design assumes the reader has the source definitions, so I mark it UNCERTAIN; if the IR is meant to be self-contained, this would be material.
